questions.title: Payment Terms and Discount Dates
questions.prompt: In Oracle Fusion Payables, how does a payment term actually determine an invoice's due date and any early-payment discount, and what happens when the invoice date doesn't cleanly fit the term's rule?
questions.modelAnswer: A payment term defines a due-date rule -- a fixed number of days from the invoice/terms date, a specific day of the month, or a 'proximate' rule that picks the nearest of several fixed dates -- plus an optional discount percentage and its own discount-days/cutoff. Due date and discount date are calculated independently from the same rule structure, applied against the invoice or terms date. When the invoice date falls after a day-of-month term's cutoff day, the term's 'months ahead' setting rolls the due date into the following month rather than producing an invalid or same-month date, so the term keeps working correctly even for invoices entered late in a period.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of a payment term as two parallel calculations running off the same starting date: one produces the due date, the other -- if the term has a discount -- produces the discount date and amount. For something like '2/10 Net 30,' the due date is 30 days out and the discount is available if paid within 10. Where people get tripped up is day-of-month terms, like 'due on the 15th.' If the invoice lands on the 20th, the term's cutoff day and months-ahead setting decide whether that rolls to next month's 15th or stays in the current month -- it's configured, not guessed, so I always check that setting on a new term before trusting it on edge-of-month invoices.
commonMistakes: Assuming due date is always invoice date plus a fixed number of days, ignoring day-of-month and proximate rules
Treating the discount date as automatically tied to the due date instead of its own independent calculation
Not knowing proximate payment terms round to the nearest of a list of fixed dates
Assuming the system will error on a late-month invoice instead of rolling the due date to the next period
keyPoints: A payment term defines a due-date rule plus an optional, independently-calculated discount
Day-of-month terms use a cutoff day and months-ahead setting to handle late-month invoice dates
Proximate terms select the nearest of several fixed dates
Discounts are computed on their own schedule, separate from the due date

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains due date calculation
Correctly explains discount calculation as independent

questions.title: Why a Supplier Needs Multiple Sites
questions.prompt: Why does a single supplier in Oracle Fusion Payables often need several supplier sites instead of one record, and what does a site actually control that the supplier header doesn't?
questions.modelAnswer: The supplier header holds entity-level identity information -- name, tax registration, classification -- that's true regardless of where or how you transact with that supplier. A supplier site is the operational unit tied to a specific business unit and address, and it's where payment terms, pay group, bank account assignment, remit-to address, and invoice/matching defaults actually live. A national supplier that ships from several locations, or does business with more than one business unit, needs a distinct site for each combination, because those sites can legitimately carry different terms or bank accounts even though they roll up to one identity at the header.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as identity versus operations. The header answers 'who is this supplier,' and that doesn't change no matter who in the company is transacting with them. The site answers 'how do we actually pay this specific location, under this specific business unit' -- and that absolutely can change. I've set up suppliers with three or four sites because they bill from different regional offices with different remit-to addresses and different bank accounts, or because two separate business units buy from the same vendor under different negotiated terms. The one thing that trips people up is realizing you literally cannot enter an invoice against a supplier with zero sites -- the site isn't optional polish, it's required before the supplier can transact at all.
commonMistakes: Thinking the supplier header controls payment terms or bank account assignment
Not realizing sites are business-unit specific
Assuming one bank account must cover every site for a supplier
Forgetting that an invoice cannot be entered without at least one site existing

Sites control terms, pay group, bank account, remit-to address, and matching defaults
One supplier can have multiple sites across different business units or locations
At least one site is required before any invoice can be entered

questions.title: Two-Way vs. Three-Way vs. Four-Way Matching
questions.prompt: Walk through what two-way, three-way, and four-way matching each actually validate on a Payables invoice, and why a company might require four-way matching for some purchase categories but not others.
questions.modelAnswer: Two-way matching checks invoice quantity and price against the purchase order only. Three-way matching adds a check against the receipt, confirming the goods were actually received before payment proceeds. Four-way matching adds an inspection or acceptance record, verifying quality, not just quantity -- a confirmed receipt only proves a box arrived, not that what's inside met specification. Companies apply four-way matching selectively to high-risk, high-value, or quality-sensitive categories like capital equipment or specialized materials, while routine, low-risk commodity purchases use two-way or three-way matching to keep invoice processing fast, since the added inspection step would be unnecessary overhead for something like office supplies.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this as a risk ladder. Two-way is fine for low-dollar, trusted-supplier purchases where price and quantity on the PO are basically all I need to confirm. Three-way is my default for anything physical, because it forces proof that receiving actually logged the goods before cash goes out the door. Four-way is the one I reserve for things where 'it arrived' doesn't mean 'it's good' -- a batch of specialized material or a piece of equipment that needs engineering sign-off. Setting four-way matching as the blanket policy for every purchase category would slow down routine buying for no real benefit, so the right design question is always 'what's the actual risk this category carries,' not 'what's the strictest control available.'
commonMistakes: Conflating a confirmed receipt with a quality inspection
Assuming every PO needs the same matching level regardless of category
Not tying the matching level to the actual risk of the purchase category
Ignoring the role of matching tolerances in letting small variances pass without a hold
keyPoints: Two-way matches invoice quantity/price to the PO
Three-way adds a receipt check for quantity received
Four-way adds an inspection/acceptance check for quality
Matching level should be set per purchase category based on actual risk

questions.title: Transaction Types vs. Transaction Sources in Receivables
questions.prompt: What's the functional difference between a Receivables transaction type and a transaction source, and why do you need both configured before you can create an invoice?
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction type defines the document class -- invoice, credit memo, debit memo -- along with its accounting behavior, including whether it posts and how AutoAccounting derives its GL segments. A transaction source defines where the document came from and how it's numbered: whether it's entered manually or imported through AutoInvoice, and which validations apply during that import. Both are mandatory on every transaction because type answers 'what kind of document is this' and source answers 'how did it get into the system and how is it numbered' -- a transaction literally can't be saved without one of each selected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as type answering 'what' and source answering 'how.' Type tells the system this is an invoice versus a credit memo, and drives the accounting behind it. Source tells the system whether a human keyed this in Receivables directly, or whether it arrived through AutoInvoice from an external billing system, and that source also governs the numbering sequence and which validations apply on the way in. A practical example: I'll usually set up one source for manual invoicing and a completely separate source for anything fed by AutoInvoice, partly so the numbering ranges never collide and partly so I can tell at a glance, just from the source, where a given transaction actually originated.

Forgetting that the source controls numbering and import validation, not the type
Assuming the type alone drives GL accounting without AutoAccounting rules
Not knowing a given source can restrict which transaction types are allowed through it

Transaction source defines origin, numbering, and import validation rules
Both are required before any transaction can be created
Sources commonly split manual entry from AutoInvoice-imported transactions

questions.title: Customer Profile Classes and Credit Limits
questions.prompt: How does a customer profile class in Receivables actually enforce a credit limit, and what happens functionally when a new order would push a customer over that limit?
questions.modelAnswer: A profile class is a template that sets default values -- credit limit, payment terms, dunning and statement cadence, and collector assignment -- for every customer account assigned to it, though individual accounts can override any of those defaults. The credit limit itself is typically checked at order entry, as part of order-to-cash or credit management processing, comparing the customer's open AR exposure plus the new order against the limit. Receivables doesn't block invoice creation for an amount already owed; it's the order that gets placed on credit hold pending review or release when the limit would be exceeded.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd clarify first that Receivables isn't the gatekeeper here -- it's the source of the limit value, but the actual stop happens earlier, typically when the order is entered and credit management checks exposure against the profile's limit. If I assign a customer to a 'Standard Wholesale' profile class with a $50,000 limit, every account under that class starts there, but I can still override the limit on one specific account if that customer negotiated different terms. When an order would push someone over, what I see in practice isn't Receivables refusing to invoice -- it's the order sitting on credit hold until someone with the right authority reviews and releases it or adjusts the limit.
commonMistakes: Assuming Receivables blocks invoice creation directly when a credit limit is breached
Not knowing a profile class is a template that individual customer accounts can override
Confusing credit limit with payment terms
Missing that the actual hold mechanism sits at order entry, not invoice creation
keyPoints: Profile class is a template setting defaults including credit limit
Individual customer accounts can override profile class defaults
Credit limit enforcement typically happens at order entry via credit management
Dunning cadence and collector assignment are also set at the profile level

questions.title: What AutoInvoice Actually Does
questions.prompt: What problem does AutoInvoice solve in Receivables, and what has to be true about the staged data before it will successfully create transactions?
questions.modelAnswer: AutoInvoice is the import engine that converts transaction data staged in interface tables -- fed from a billing system, a project billing module, or any other feeder system -- into real Receivables transactions in bulk, instead of someone keying each invoice manually. For a row to succeed, it needs a valid, resolvable transaction source and type combination, a customer and bill-to site that actually resolve, line/tax/freight amounts that balance, and accounting segments that are either supplied or derivable through AutoAccounting. Rows that fail any of these checks don't silently vanish -- they land in a rejections area with a specific, identifiable reason.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it: AutoInvoice exists because nobody wants to manually key thousands of invoices that already exist, correctly formed, in some other billing system. My job when I run it is mostly about what happens afterward -- checking the AutoInvoice execution and exception report for anything that didn't make it through clean. The rejections I see most often are an invalid customer or bill-to site reference, a transaction source/type combination that isn't actually valid together, or a GL date that falls in a period that's already closed. The fix-and-resubmit workflow is the normal rhythm here -- correct the staged row, resubmit just that row, and move on, rather than treating one rejection as a reason to distrust the whole batch.
commonMistakes: Assuming AutoInvoice works like a simple CSV import with no validation
Not knowing rejected rows stay in the interface table for correction and resubmission
Forgetting the transaction source must match what AutoInvoice is told to process
Ignoring that tax and freight amounts must also validate, not just the line amount
keyPoints: AutoInvoice bulk-converts staged feeder data into real Receivables transactions
Requires a valid customer/site, source/type combination, and balanced amounts
Rejections are reported with specific reasons, not silent failures
Supports correcting and resubmitting just the failed rows

questions.title: Bank Account Uses and Why They're Business-Unit Specific
questions.prompt: What does a 'bank account use' control in Cash Management, and why would the same physical bank account need to be set up for use by multiple business units or modules?
questions.modelAnswer: A bank account is defined once at the bank, branch, and account level, but a 'use' is what actually grants a specific business unit and module -- Payables for disbursement, Receivables for receipts, payroll, and so on -- permission to transact against it. This separation lets one physical account be shared across business units or purposes without duplicating the account setup, while still controlling, use by use, exactly which BU/module combination can issue a payment or record a receipt from it. Bank account security then adds a further layer restricting which individual users or roles can even select that account at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I picture the account itself as a filing cabinet that exists once, and each 'use' as a key that lets a specific business unit and module open a specific drawer in it. A single operating account might have one use letting Payables disburse from it and a completely separate use letting Receivables record deposits into it -- each use independently assignable and revocable without touching the underlying account record. Beyond that, bank account security decides which actual people or roles can select the account on a transaction at all, which is a different control layer from the use itself -- having a use configured doesn't mean every user automatically sees that account in a payment screen.

questions.title: Reconciliation Rules vs. Matching Rules
questions.prompt: In Cash Management, what's the difference between a reconciliation rule set and a matching rule, and why does automatic reconciliation depend on both being configured correctly?
questions.modelAnswer: A matching rule defines how a bank statement line is compared against system transactions -- amount tolerance, date tolerance, reference-number matching -- to decide whether they represent the same event. A reconciliation rule set groups matching rules together with the transaction sources they apply to and the order they're tried in. Automatic reconciliation depends on both because the rule set decides which transactions are even eligible candidates and in what sequence, while the matching rule inside it decides whether a given candidate actually counts as a match. A correct rule set paired with a badly tuned matching rule will either over-match incorrectly or leave legitimate matches sitting unreconciled.
questions.professionalAnswer: When reconciliation isn't behaving the way I expect, I separate these two questions in my head: is the right stuff even being considered (that's the rule set), and is the comparison logic itself too loose or too tight (that's the matching rule). I usually start a new bank account's tolerances tight -- a small dollar and day window -- then watch what lands in the exceptions report for a cycle or two. If I keep seeing a consistent one-day lag from a particular bank feed that should obviously be a match, I'll loosen the date tolerance slightly rather than leaving good transactions unreconciled every month for a pattern I already understand.
commonMistakes: Treating 'reconciliation rule' and 'matching rule' as the same setting
Not realizing the rule set determines which transaction sources are even eligible
Assuming one global matching rule applies to every bank account
Not tuning tolerances based on real exception review
keyPoints: Matching rule defines how lines are compared, via tolerances and references
Reconciliation rule set defines which sources and order are eligible
Both are required for automatic reconciliation to work correctly
Tolerances should be tuned from real, observed exception patterns

questions.title: Choosing a Depreciation Method
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between straight-line and an accelerated depreciation method like declining balance in Oracle Fusion Assets, and why might a company run different methods in its corporate book versus its tax book for the same asset?
questions.modelAnswer: Straight-line expenses an equal amount every period across the asset's useful life. An accelerated method like declining balance expenses more in the early periods and less later, reflecting faster early value loss or front-loading deductions. A company commonly runs straight-line in its corporate book for a predictable, consistent GAAP expense pattern, while using an accelerated method permitted by tax law in its tax book to maximize early tax deductions. Both calculations draw from the same underlying asset cost and life data, so the same physical asset can legitimately depreciate differently in each book without being entered twice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through a concrete case: a company buys equipment, and I add it once in the corporate book using straight-line, because that gives a smooth, predictable expense for external financial statements. When that addition gets mass-copied to the associated tax book, I'm free to let the tax book apply an accelerated method the tax code permits, front-loading deductions in the early years. What I want someone to understand is that this isn't two separate assets with two separate stories -- it's one asset, one source cost, with two books independently applying whatever depreciation treatment actually fits their reporting purpose.
commonMistakes: Assuming an asset can only use one depreciation method across every book
Not explaining why accelerated methods benefit tax reporting
Confusing depreciation method with prorate convention
Missing that corporate and tax books share the same source asset cost data
keyPoints: Straight-line produces even expense; accelerated methods front-load expense
Corporate and tax books commonly use different methods for different purposes

questions.title: Corporate Book vs. Tax Book
questions.prompt: What's the structural relationship between a corporate depreciation book and a tax book in Oracle Fusion Assets -- are they independent sets of asset records, or something else?
questions.modelAnswer: A tax book is associated with, and derives from, a corporate book -- it isn't an independent set of asset records. Additions entered in the corporate book can be mass-copied into the associated tax book, after which the tax book maintains its own depreciation method, life, and convention independently going forward. This design means a single physical asset addition flows into both books without duplicate manual entry, while still allowing the books to diverge in treatment afterward, because they serve different reporting purposes -- GAAP financial statements versus tax filings.
questions.professionalAnswer: My usual workflow is to add the asset exactly once, in the corporate book, with its real cost and date placed in service. From there I run the mass copy process into the associated tax book, which brings the addition over without me re-keying anything. After that copy, the two books are genuinely independent -- I can adjust the tax book's life or method without that touching the corporate book's depreciation at all. The thing people sometimes assume incorrectly is that this means every asset needs manual duplicate entry per book; it's actually built specifically to avoid that, with mass copy as the connecting mechanism.

questions.title: How Expense Policies and Limits Actually Get Enforced
questions.prompt: When an expense policy sets a per-night hotel limit, how does Oracle Fusion Expenses actually enforce that at the point an employee submits a report, and what happens to an amount over the limit?
questions.modelAnswer: Policy limits attach to expense types or templates and are checked against submitted line amounts at submission. Depending on how the policy is configured, an over-limit amount can be flagged as a violation requiring justification, split into a reimbursable portion up to the limit plus a non-reimbursable or employee-liable overage, or routed into mandatory approval rather than auto-approved. The system surfaces the violation for a reviewer or the policy's defined action to resolve -- it doesn't silently truncate the reimbursed amount without a record of what happened.
questions.professionalAnswer: I set these up thinking about what a reviewer actually needs to see, not just a number that silently gets capped. A per-night hotel limit configured on the expense type checks each submitted line as it comes in, and if someone's over, I want that flagged -- maybe requiring a justification note or the receipt image -- rather than the system quietly reimbursing only the capped amount with no explanation. Whether the configured action is 'require approval,' 'split the amount,' or something else depends on company policy, but the common thread is that an over-limit line should always be visible and explainable, never just a silent reduction.

questions.title: Company-Pay vs. Individual-Pay Corporate Card Transactions
questions.prompt: What's the functional difference between a 'company pay' and an 'individual pay' corporate card transaction in Oracle Fusion Expenses, and why does that distinction matter for how the expense report gets reimbursed?
questions.modelAnswer: Company-pay transactions are billed directly to and settled by the company, so when an employee includes that charge on an expense report, no reimbursement is owed to them for that line -- it's purely an accounting entry allocating the expense. Individual-pay transactions are charged to a card the employee personally pays off, so the corresponding line does generate a reimbursement once approved. Because the pay type determines whether a line flows into the employee's reimbursement at all, misclassifying a card program this way would either underpay or overpay the employee relative to what they actually owe personally.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always check the card program's pay type before assuming how a report will settle, because the two types behave completely differently on the same report. A company-liability card used for airfare the company already paid for is company-pay -- that line shows up for expense tracking and accounting, but the employee isn't owed anything for it. A personal-liability card the employee swipes and pays off themselves is individual-pay, and that line absolutely does generate a reimbursement. It's entirely normal to see both types on one report, which is exactly why I don't assume every card charge automatically means money is owed back to the employee.

questions.title: OTBI, BI Publisher, Financial Reporting Center, or Smart View
questions.prompt: Given four reporting tools available in Oracle Fusion Financials -- OTBI, BI Publisher, Financial Reporting Center, and Smart View -- how do you decide which one actually fits a given reporting request?
questions.modelAnswer: Financial Reporting Center, using Financial Report Studio, is built for formatted, grid-based financial statements like a balance sheet or income statement with GL balances driving row/column logic. OTBI is for ad hoc, self-service analysis and dashboards across transactional subject areas, suited to exploration rather than a fixed statement layout. BI Publisher is for pixel-perfect, templated output -- an invoice, a check, a regulatory form -- where exact layout and scheduled distribution to many recipients matters. Smart View is for pulling live GL/FR data directly into Excel for ad hoc modeling using a familiar spreadsheet interface. The deciding factor is the audience and the shape of the required output, not personal familiarity with one tool.
questions.professionalAnswer: When someone brings me a reporting request, I ask what the output actually needs to look like and who's going to use it. A monthly balance sheet and income statement package for the CFO is Financial Reporting Center -- it needs a consistent formatted structure every period. A controller who wants to slice AP aging by supplier and region on their own, differently each time, is OTBI -- the point is letting them explore without me rebuilding anything. Printing checks or remittance advices in an exact required layout is BI Publisher's job. And an FP&A analyst who wants to pull live numbers into a model they're already building in Excel is Smart View. Picking the wrong one usually means fighting the tool instead of using it.

questions.title: Setting Up a New Supplier End-to-End
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, how you'd set up a brand-new supplier in Oracle Fusion Payables so it's actually ready to receive an invoice and get paid -- not just the header record.
questions.modelAnswer: First create the supplier header -- name, tax registration/TIN, supplier type or classification. Next create at least one supplier site tied to the correct business unit, specifying address, payment terms, pay group, and invoice/matching defaults. Verify the site is enabled for whatever procurement business unit will reference it on purchase orders. Finally, run a small test invoice or review to confirm the supplier can actually be selected and matched correctly before relying on it for a real payment run.

My sequence is always header, then at least one site with the right BU and terms, then a bank account attached to that specific site so electronic payment works instead of silently falling back or failing. If the supplier is a 1099 vendor, I populate the classification fields now, because skipping that creates real cleanup work at tax time rather than at setup time. Before I call it done, I'll pull up the supplier on a test invoice just to confirm matching and payment method actually behave the way I expect, rather than trusting the setup screens alone.

questions.title: Entering an Invoice with Multiple Distributions
questions.prompt: You need to enter a standard invoice for $12,000 that should be split 60/40 across two cost centers. Walk through how you'd actually enter this in Payables so the distributions are correct before validation.

questions.title: Matching an Invoice to a PO and Receipt
questions.prompt: A supplier invoice has come in for a PO-backed purchase, and the receiving department has already recorded a receipt. Walk through how you'd actually perform three-way matching on this invoice in Payables.
questions.modelAnswer: On the invoice, select 'Match to PO' and identify the correct PO number and line. Payables pulls in the PO's price and the already-recorded receipt quantity, then compares the invoice quantity and price against both within configured tolerances. If the invoice quantity exceeds what's been received, or the price exceeds the PO price beyond tolerance, a matching hold is placed automatically rather than letting the invoice validate clean. If everything's within tolerance, the match completes and distributions are generated automatically from the PO's account coding instead of manual entry.

questions.title: An Asset Isn't Picking Up Depreciation This Period
questions.prompt: You run depreciation for the period, and one specific asset that should clearly be depreciating shows zero expense. What would you check?
questions.modelAnswer: Check the asset's date placed in service against the prorate convention -- if the date falls after the convention's cutoff for this period, the asset legitimately doesn't start depreciating until next period, which isn't an error. Check whether the asset is actually capitalized in this book, since an asset still sitting in CIP, or in a different book than the one being checked, won't depreciate in the book under review. Check whether the asset has already been fully depreciated or whether its method/life combination produces zero expense for this specific period. Check whether the asset was recently transferred, retired, or had a cost adjustment affecting current-period processing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat zero depreciation as probably explainable before I treat it as a bug. The two checks that resolve this most often are the date placed in service against the prorate convention, and whether the asset is actually capitalized in the book I'm looking at rather than still sitting in CIP or living in a different book. If both of those look fine, I check whether the method and life combination could legitimately produce a near-zero expense this period, and then whether there's a recent transfer, retirement, or cost adjustment that explains it. Only after all of that comes up clean would I suspect an actual data problem.

Forgetting the asset might legitimately have no expense this period due to its method/life
Not checking for a recent transfer, retirement, or adjustment affecting the current period

questions.title: An Employee's Expense Reports Keep Getting Flagged by Audit Rules
questions.prompt: An employee complains their expense reports are constantly getting flagged for manager review, even for routine expenses, and it's slowing down their reimbursements. How would you investigate whether this is a real policy pattern or a configuration problem?
questions.modelAnswer: Review the specific audit rules actually firing on their reports and the exact condition each one checks, rather than assuming the employee is doing something wrong -- a rule meant to catch unusually large meals might accidentally catch a normal group dinner because it doesn't account for attendee count. Compare the flagged lines against the actual written policy to determine whether the rule is correctly enforcing policy or has a configuration gap. If the rule is working as designed and the employee really is near a legitimate threshold repeatedly, that's a real pattern worth discussing with them directly rather than a system problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat a complaint like this as useful signal about rule tuning, not just a one-off employee issue. I pull up the specific rule and condition that's actually firing and compare it against real flagged examples -- often what's happening is the rule's scope is broader than intended, like a meal threshold that doesn't account for attendee count and ends up catching ordinary group dinners. If the rule turns out to be over-broad, I fix it for everyone, not just quietly exempt this one employee. If it turns out the employee really is near a legitimate threshold repeatedly, that's a different, honest conversation to have with them directly.

Not checking whether the audit rule's scope/threshold is correctly tuned against real examples
Fixing it ad hoc for one employee instead of correcting a genuinely over-broad rule for everyone
Not distinguishing a configuration problem from a real recurring policy pattern

Compare flagged lines against written policy to check correct scoping
An over-broad rule should be corrected for everyone, not patched around for one employee
Distinguish a real recurring pattern from a configuration gap

questions.title: An Employee's Corporate Card Charges Aren't Showing Up
questions.prompt: An employee says their corporate card charges from last week still haven't appeared for them to add to an expense report. What would you check?
questions.modelAnswer: Check the card feed and transaction load schedule from the card issuer, since most corporate card integrations load on a batch schedule rather than in real time, and a very recent charge may simply not have loaded yet. Check whether the employee's card is correctly linked to their user profile in Expenses, since a mapping gap means transactions load but never associate with that employee. Check whether the transactions loaded but are sitting in an exception or unassigned queue due to a card number or employee ID mismatch. Only after ruling out load timing and mapping issues should an actual feed failure be suspected.
questions.professionalAnswer: Load timing is almost always my first check, since these feeds typically load on a daily or near-daily batch, not instantly -- a charge from a few days ago being missing is very different from one that's been missing for two weeks. If enough time has passed that timing alone doesn't explain it, I check whether the employee's card is actually mapped to their profile correctly, and whether there's a mismatch sending their transactions into an unassigned exception queue instead of to them directly. I'd only escalate to the card issuer's integration as an actual feed failure after ruling out these simpler, far more common explanations.

Not checking whether the employee's card is correctly mapped to their profile
Missing that mismatched transactions can land in an exception queue instead of simply being lost
Escalating to integration support before ruling out the simpler, more common causes

Check for transactions sitting in an exception/unassigned queue due to a mismatch
Treat an actual feed failure as the last explanation, not the first assumption

questions.title: An OTBI Analysis Doesn't Match the Subledger
questions.prompt: A finance analyst says their OTBI analysis of AP invoice amounts doesn't match what they see directly in Payables. Walk through how you'd investigate the discrepancy.
questions.modelAnswer: Check the analysis's filters and prompts first, since a date range, status filter, or business unit scope narrower or different than what the analyst expects in Payables is the most common reason the numbers don't match. Check whether OTBI is reporting against real-time transactional data for this subject area or a periodically refreshed extract, since a refresh lag would explain a temporary mismatch. Check for a difference in what's actually being measured, such as OTBI showing invoice header amount while the analyst expects a distribution-level or tax-inclusive figure. Only after ruling out filter, refresh timing, and definitional differences should a genuine data or security issue be suspected.

I walk the analyst through exactly what filters and prompts are applied to their analysis, since a narrower date range or BU scope than what they're comparing against in Payables explains a lot of these. I also check whether the subject area refreshes on a schedule rather than showing real-time data, and whether the measure itself -- header amount versus a distribution-level figure -- is actually the same thing the analyst is comparing it to. I only escalate as a data integrity issue once all of that is ruled out.

Check for a definitional difference in what's being measured

questions.title: How Payables Transactions Actually Reach the General Ledger
questions.prompt: Walk through, architecturally, the path a validated Payables invoice takes before its accounting ever shows up as a journal in the General Ledger.
questions.modelAnswer: Once an invoice validates, Create Accounting -- built on Subledger Accounting rules -- generates detailed subledger journal entries from the invoice distributions, applying the accounting method configured for the ledger. This subledger-level detail supports drill-back from a GL balance to the originating transaction. The Payables to General Ledger transfer process then moves those subledger journals into actual GL journal batches, which still require posting in GL before they affect account balances. This layered design, with Subledger Accounting as a rules-driven intermediate layer rather than Payables writing directly to GL, enables drill-back and consistent accounting treatment across every subledger feeding the same GL.
questions.professionalAnswer: When a GL balance looks wrong and someone wants to trace it back, this layered design is exactly what makes that possible. I think of it as invoice, then subledger accounting generates the detailed journal under rules specific to the ledger, then the transfer process moves that into GL, which still needs posting before it actually affects a balance. If a number looks off, I chase it through that exact chain -- invoice distribution, subledger journal, GL transfer, GL posting -- rather than assuming Payables wrote something directly and wrongly to GL, because it never does that directly in the first place.

Not knowing Subledger Accounting is a shared, rules-driven engine used by multiple subledgers
Forgetting the GL transfer still requires a separate posting step
Missing the drill-back/audit benefit this architecture provides

This layer supports drill-back from GL to the originating transaction
The GL transfer process moves subledger journals into GL, which still requires posting
The same architecture is shared across AP, AR, Fixed Assets, and other subledgers

questions.title: Why Receivables Is Built on the Trading Community Model
questions.prompt: Why does Oracle Fusion model customers through 'parties, accounts, and sites' instead of a single flat customer record, and what architectural problem does that solve?
questions.modelAnswer: The Trading Community Model separates the real-world entity, a party that can exist independent of any specific business relationship, from the business relationship with that entity, an account representing how you transact with them, from the physical locations tied to that relationship, the sites. This separation solves the problem of one real-world entity needing multiple distinct business relationships -- the same company could be both a customer and a supplier, or have separate accounts for different business units -- without duplicating or conflating identity data, letting a party's core identity stay consistent while accounts and sites vary per relationship.
questions.professionalAnswer: The example that makes this click for me is a large conglomerate that's both a customer buying from us and, separately, a supplier we buy from. The same underlying party record anchors both relationships, while the account layer keeps the customer-side relationship, terms, and transactions cleanly separate from the supplier-side one, instead of forcing one flat record to awkwardly represent two completely different kinds of relationships. Sites then sit under an account specifically for the physical bill-to/ship-to detail. It looks like extra complexity until you hit that exact scenario, and then it's obviously the right structure.
commonMistakes: Describing the party/account/site split as unnecessary complexity rather than a deliberate solution to a real identity problem
Not explaining that one party can have multiple accounts for different relationships or business units
Confusing account with site
Missing the dual customer/supplier relationship scenario as the clearest justification
keyPoints: Party is the real-world entity's identity, independent of any specific relationship
Account is a specific business relationship with that party
Site is a physical location tied to an account
This separation supports one entity having multiple, distinct relationships without duplicating identity data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the party/account/site layers

Gives a realistic scenario such as the same entity as customer and supplier

questions.title: Designing Revenue Recognition Rules in Receivables
questions.prompt: A company sells a product bundled with a year of support that should be recognized ratably, not all at invoice date. How would you think through setting this up architecturally in Receivables?
questions.modelAnswer: This requires a revenue recognition rule at the transaction line level that spreads recognized revenue across the support period rather than recognizing it all at invoice date. The invoice can still bill the customer up front, since billing and revenue recognition timing are deliberately decoupled in this architecture, while the accounting generated through Subledger Accounting defers the support line's revenue into a deferred revenue account and recognizes it ratably across the covered periods. The product line, recognized immediately, and the support line, recognized ratably, need distinct setups and distinct rules so each line's accounting behaves independently even on the same invoice.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key design insight is that billing and revenue recognition are deliberately separate concerns here -- the customer gets billed the full amount up front for cash flow purposes, but the accounting follows its own schedule, which is exactly what rules like ASC 606 require. For this bundle, I'd set the product line to recognize immediately and the support line to use a ratable recognition rule spreading revenue evenly across the twelve months, with a deferred revenue account holding the not-yet-recognized portion in the interim. Both lines sit on the same invoice but follow completely independent accounting timelines.

Not setting up a distinct rule for the ratably-recognized line versus the immediately-recognized line
Forgetting deferred revenue accounts are involved in the interim period
Treating this as a reporting-only concern rather than something configured at the transaction/accounting rule level

A revenue recognition rule on the line defines the ratable schedule
Deferred revenue accounts hold the not-yet-recognized portion
Different lines on the same invoice can follow different recognition rules

questions.title: Where Cash Management Sits Between AP, AR, and GL
questions.prompt: Cash Management isn't where payments or receipts originate, and it isn't the General Ledger either. Architecturally, what role does it actually play in the overall Financials picture?
questions.modelAnswer: Cash Management sits as a verification and treasury layer that consumes transactions already created elsewhere -- payments from Payables, receipts from Receivables, and manual journal entries from GL -- and reconciles them against the bank's own record of activity. It doesn't originate AP/AR transactions, and it doesn't post to GL directly. Its core job is confirming that what the subledgers believe happened financially actually matches what the bank confirms happened, surfacing exceptions like an unrecorded bank fee or a payment that never cleared back to the owning module for correction, while feeding cash positioning and forecasting from this reconciled data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe Cash Management as the control point that catches discrepancies between what AP, AR, and GL think happened and what the bank actually says happened -- it's an independent check, not a transaction-originating module. That separation is deliberate: the module that creates a payment isn't the same module that confirms it actually cleared, which is a real internal control, not an accidental design choice. Once reconciliation confirms the data is trustworthy, that same verified data is what feeds cash positioning and forecasting, so the whole treasury picture rests on Cash Management having done its reconciliation job correctly first.

Missing the separation-of-duties/internal-control rationale for having an independent reconciliation layer
Not mentioning that reconciled data feeds cash positioning/forecasting

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Book Fixed Assets Structure
questions.prompt: A company needs to track assets for GAAP financial reporting, for tax filings using a different depreciation method, and for internal capital budgeting comparisons. How would you think through structuring the asset books to support all three?
questions.modelAnswer: Structure a corporate book as the primary book reflecting GAAP depreciation treatment and feeding the General Ledger. Associate one or more tax books to the corporate book so capitalized additions flow over via mass copy without duplicate entry, letting the tax book apply its own tax-permitted method and life independently afterward. Add a budget book, not tied to real GL postings, to model hypothetical or forecasted capital scenarios using projected additions and depreciation assumptions. This three-book structure lets one set of physical assets support three genuinely different reporting purposes from a shared source of asset data rather than three disconnected registers.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this around one principle: a single physical asset shouldn't need to be entered three separate times just because three different audiences need to see it differently. The corporate book carries the real GAAP depreciation and feeds GL. A tax book associates to it and picks up additions through mass copy, then is free to apply an accelerated method the tax code allows, completely independent of the corporate book going forward. A budget book sits apart from both, with no real GL impact at all, purely for modeling what-if capital scenarios. The tradeoff worth flagging is that once these books diverge, someone has to deliberately maintain that divergence -- it doesn't happen automatically after the initial copy.

Not knowing budget books don't post to GL
Forgetting tax books still derive from corporate book additions via mass copy rather than independent entry
Missing the underlying rationale of one real asset supporting multiple valid reporting treatments

questions.title: Designing Asset Categories So Depreciation Defaults Actually Work
questions.prompt: A finance team wants new asset additions to automatically get the right depreciation method, life, and GL accounts without someone manually setting those every time. How would you design the asset category structure to make that happen?
questions.modelAnswer: Design asset categories, meaning major and minor category combinations, that correspond to the real distinct classes of assets the business owns, such as computer equipment, vehicles, and buildings. Configure category defaults, including default depreciation method, life, prorate convention, and default GL account segments per book, directly on the category so any new addition assigned to it automatically inherits correct setup. Keep the category list granular enough to reflect genuinely different depreciation treatments, since vehicles depreciate differently than buildings, but not so granular that nearly-identical asset types are needlessly split, which creates unnecessary maintenance.

I design categories around actual depreciation treatment differences, not around departmental or organizational lines, and I remember category defaults are set per book, so the same category can legitimately carry different defaults in the corporate book versus the tax book. Periodically reviewing real additions against the category structure tells me whether it's actually working or just looks right on paper.

questions.title: How an Approved Expense Report Becomes a Real Payment and Journal Entry
questions.prompt: Walk through, architecturally, what actually happens between an employee's expense report getting final approval and the company's GL reflecting that expense and the employee getting reimbursed.
questions.modelAnswer: Once an expense report is fully approved, it's processed into an invoice-like record in Payables, since Expenses hands the reimbursement obligation to the module actually built for issuing payments to a payee rather than paying employees directly. Payables then processes that reimbursement through its normal payment cycle -- a payment process request, bank account, payment method -- just as it would for a supplier payment. Accounting for the underlying expense is generated via Subledger Accounting rules tied to the expense types/accounts on the report, flowing to GL through the same Payables-to-GL transfer path used for ordinary supplier invoices.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I find clarifying here is that Expenses doesn't have its own separate payment engine at all -- once a report is approved, it's handed to Payables, which treats the employee functionally like a payee the same way it would a supplier. That reuse means the reimbursement goes through the exact same payment process request, bank account, and payment method setup as a supplier payment, and the accounting flows through the same Subledger Accounting and GL transfer path too. It's a deliberate choice to avoid building and maintaining a second payment infrastructure just for employee reimbursements.

questions.title: Designing Reporting Delivery for Three Different Audiences
questions.prompt: The CFO wants a fixed monthly financial statement package, a regional controller wants to explore AP spend interactively, and a bank requires a specific regulatory filing format. Architecturally, how would you decide what to build for each?
questions.modelAnswer: For the CFO's fixed monthly package, build it in Financial Reporting Center using Financial Report Studio, since the output needs a consistent formatted financial-statement structure every period. questions.title: Designing an OTBI Dashboard for Multiple Finance Stakeholders

questions.title: Why BI Publisher Separates the Data Model From the Report Template
questions.prompt: BI Publisher deliberately splits a report into a data model and a separate template. What architectural problem does that separation solve, and when would you actually need to change one without touching the other?
questions.modelAnswer: The data model defines what data is retrieved -- the query or data source and its structure -- while the template defines how that data is laid out and formatted for a specific output, such as a government form's exact layout or a branded invoice design. Separating them means the same underlying data model can serve multiple different templates, and a single template's visual design can be updated without touching or re-testing the underlying query logic at all -- this decoupling is what makes report maintenance manageable at scale instead of every formatting tweak risking a change to the data logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: The scenario that justifies this split clearly is a regulatory form where the agency tweaks their required layout slightly. questions.title: Explaining a Payment Delay to an Impatient Supplier
questions.prompt: A supplier calls, frustrated that their invoice hasn't been paid yet, and you can see it's sitting on a legitimate three-way matching hold because the receipt quantity doesn't match what they invoiced. How do you handle this conversation?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer stays calm and factual rather than over-promising a timeline that isn't realistic, or being dismissive of the supplier's frustration. It explains, in plain terms the supplier can act on, specifically what's holding the invoice -- a quantity mismatch against what receiving recorded -- without unilaterally blaming either party, and gives them something concrete to do, such as confirming the shipped quantity on their end or coordinating with receiving to resolve the discrepancy, rather than just saying 'it's stuck, I'll look into it.' It also sets a realistic expectation for when they'll hear back, and actually follows through on that timeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd acknowledge the supplier's frustration genuinely without getting defensive, then explain the specific hold reason in plain language -- the quantity on the invoice doesn't match what receiving logged. I'd propose a concrete next step, like comparing their shipping documentation against our receipt record together, and commit to a specific follow-up time rather than a vague 'soon.' questions.title: A Difficult Collections Call With an Overdue Customer
questions.prompt: You need to call a customer whose invoice is now 45 days past due, and they've been difficult to reach and vague in prior emails. How do you approach this call?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer prepares before dialing -- knowing the specific invoice amounts, dates, and any prior promises the customer already made and didn't keep -- rather than going in generic. The call itself should be direct and professional, stating the specific overdue amount and asking directly what's preventing payment, while actually listening for a real reason, such as a dispute, a cash-flow problem, or a lost invoice, that changes the right next step. It should end with a specific, documented commitment, like an exact payment date or a resolution plan for a dispute, rather than another vague assurance, and that commitment should be followed up on the agreed date.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I call, I review the account's actual history and any prior promises that weren't kept, so I'm not going in cold. On the call, I'm direct about the overdue amount and ask plainly what's holding up payment, rather than being apologetic about simply asking for money owed. I listen carefully for whether this is a genuine dispute over the invoice, a cash-flow problem, or avoidance, because each one needs a different response. I don't accept another vague 'soon' -- I push for a specific dated commitment, write it down, and then actually follow up exactly on that date, since a collections contact who reliably follows through gets taken more seriously over time.
commonMistakes: Going into the call without reviewing the account's actual history and prior promises
Being vague or apologetic about asking for payment instead of being direct and professional
Accepting another non-specific promise instead of pushing for a dated commitment
Not following up at the agreed time, which undermines future collections credibility
keyPoints: Prepare with the account's specific history and prior broken promises before calling
Be direct and professional about the overdue amount rather than vague
Listen for and distinguish the real underlying cause
Close with a specific, dated commitment and follow up exactly then

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows preparation with account history
Communicates directly and professionally
Listens for and distinguishes the real underlying cause
Secures a specific dated commitment and follows through

questions.title: Accounting Disagrees With How an Asset Is Being Capitalized
questions.prompt: The controller believes a large renovation project should be capitalized as a fixed asset, but you believe part of it is really a repair expense that shouldn't be capitalized. How do you raise this disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't silently capitalize it the controller's way to avoid friction, nor dig in stubbornly without evidence -- it brings the specific capitalization criteria, such as whether the cost extends useful life or meaningfully improves the asset versus simply restoring it to normal working condition, and applies that test to the actual invoice or work breakdown, showing concretely which line items look like capital improvement and which look like routine repair. It raises this as a question grounded in policy and real cost detail, invites the controller's reasoning since they may know project context that changes the analysis, and stays genuinely open to being convinced either way by the facts.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go in with the actual cost breakdown and the capitalization criteria side by side, not just a gut feeling that something feels off. I'd frame it as 'let's apply the test together to these specific line items' rather than a flat disagreement, pointing to which costs look like they extend the asset's life or improve it versus which look like they just restore normal working condition. I'd genuinely invite the controller's perspective, since they might know something about the project's scope that changes the right answer, and I'd be fully willing to update my own conclusion once we've actually looked at the facts together.
commonMistakes: Silently going along with the wrong treatment to avoid conflict
Asserting a different view without grounding it in the actual capitalization criteria and cost detail
Treating the disagreement as personal rather than a shared application of policy to facts
Not being open to the controller's additional context changing the conclusion
keyPoints: Ground the disagreement in the actual capitalization criteria applied to specific cost line items
Present the analysis as a shared application of policy rather than a personal position
Invite the other person's context/reasoning genuinely
Stay open to being wrong once more facts are on the table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the disagreement in specific criteria and cost detail
Frames the conversation collaboratively rather than combatively
Genuinely invites the other person's reasoning/context
Shows openness to revising the conclusion based on facts
